lxc_c194055c6c6d615d.text: Finland’s story includes ancient settlement, Swedish and Russian rule, independence, war, and rapid modern development.

lxc_d87cdaee7d097015.text: Its people, languages, and national identity formed through many changes—not from one simple migration.

lxc_e7b7797e864e9e01.text: One way to approach this history is to ask: what written records exist, where did the people come from, and how did names and languages change over time?

lxc_d77b5eb594c31dc0.text: The first known written mention of the *Fenni* comes from the Roman writer Tacitus in 98 CE.

lxc_d337bbed9f54cfd7.text: However, his description of northern hunter-gatherers does not prove that they were the ancestors of modern Finns.

lxc_ebec5b00017e8a13.text: Even the origins of the names *Finland* and *Suomi* remain uncertain.

lxc_58f69d1e58356ef0.text: Archaeology shows continuous settlement in Finland since about 9000 BCE, but languages and people also moved over time.

lxc_24721001856a3ebe.text: Ancestors of Finnish speakers came west in several waves.

lxc_445436c7b5748f1d.text: Finnish developed from Proto-Finnic, probably spoken south of the Gulf of Finland.

lxc_5510100e85d518d3.text: It belongs to the Uralic family and is closely related to Estonian and Karelian—not to Indo-European languages such as Lithuanian.

lxc_5f98025c3db6474d.text: Sámi languages were once spoken across much more of Finland.

lxc_6ca54194bcfd334c.text: From the late 13th century, most Finnish lands became part of Sweden.

lxc_332ea3fed2b8e2ec.text: Turku was the main town, and Swedish was used in government, education, and elite life.

lxc_bc3f3f178f154eb5.text: In the 16th century, bishop Mikael Agricola created the first comprehensive Finnish writing system.

lxc_7f74fd2cbb998ec6.text: His *Abckiria* primer appeared in 1543, and his Finnish New Testament in 1551.

lxc_6c3df665d31f01c7.text: Swedish rule ended after the Finnish War of 1808–1809.

lxc_b9483f64ff069ea7.text: Finland then became an autonomous Grand Duchy within the Russian Empire.

lxc_71cf171cba9967f4.text: It kept many Swedish laws, while Helsinki became the capital in 1812.

lxc_337c74562cad492d.text: Finnish national culture also grew: Elias Lönnrot published the *Kalevala* in 1835, and an 1863 language decree began raising Finnish toward official status.

lxc_49081d16b55c1495.text: In 1906, Finland created a one-chamber parliament and became the first European country to give women both the vote and the right to stand for election.

lxc_7c94ad1f5cf5c6fa.text: The Russian Revolution opened a path to independence.

lxc_ea14d2575f017830.text: Finland’s Senate presented a declaration in December 1917, and Parliament accepted it on 6 December by 100 votes to 88.

lxc_5444ae3909017f34.text: Soviet Russia recognised Finland soon afterward.

lxc_e6d48a4d9815a623.text: Finland still celebrates 6 December as Independence Day.

lxc_d0769590d5b76d8d.text: However, the new country quickly divided.

lxc_a8e2f4d94e39c044.text: From January to May 1918, the socialist Reds fought the government-supported Whites.

lxc_68281b60f5c7ae9d.text: The Whites won with help from German troops.

lxc_26ca18e3f51e2145.text: The Battle of Tampere was the bloodiest battle, and prison camps caused many later deaths from hunger and disease.

lxc_5218339155c2d0f8.text: Altogether, about 38,000 people died in a population of roughly three million.

lxc_d8afbe35768acd79.text: The conflict left deep political and social wounds.

lxc_2ac85fbbab161534.text: Nevertheless, Finland adopted a republican constitution in 1919, and Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg became its first president.

lxc_52cbf4a3ae3d7e5e.text: The Soviet Union invaded Finland on 30 November 1939, beginning the Winter War.

lxc_e29a20d5529a6508.text: Although Finland had a much smaller army, Finnish forces stopped or defeated Soviet units in places such as Suomussalmi and Raate Road.

lxc_affd2cea5c054f42.text: Finland remained independent but gave up about nine percent of its land, and more than 422,000 Karelians were evacuated.

lxc_b26d09e553408cab.text: Finland fought the Soviet Union again in the Continuation War from 1941 to 1944, this time alongside Germany as a co-belligerent.

lxc_30ea2be1b5898c00.text: A major Soviet offensive captured Viipuri in June 1944, but Finnish forces stopped further advances at battles including Tali-Ihantala.

lxc_e9efddba1536160a.text: The armistice required Finland to give up more territory and then remove German troops from Lapland.

lxc_c2dc0999687d53f0.text: Across the two Soviet wars, Finland lost about 12 percent of its land, but it was not occupied and its democratic state survived.

lxc_8203a558b253dc98.text: Modern Finland is a Nordic republic of about 5.6–5.7 million people.

lxc_4d9ca0075e0700a3.text: Finnish and Swedish are its national languages, while Northern, Inari, and Skolt Sámi have official status in parts of the Sámi homeland.

lxc_4d37e69762c0695f.text: This language map reflects the country’s layered history.

lxc_bd77596c704097b6.text: Nature is central to Finland’s image: forests cover most of the land, and official counts include 187,888 lakes larger than 500 square metres.

lxc_8fb512b7c037ea53.text: Sauna is another strong cultural symbol.

lxc_5eeca763a45a9630.text: Finland has about 3.2 million saunas, and Finnish sauna culture entered UNESCO’s intangible heritage list in 2020.

lxc_62a98f29ee21b3ae.text: Finland joined the European Union in 1995 and adopted euro cash in 2002.

lxc_7f2045218edb46cb.text: After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Finland changed its security policy and applied to NATO.

lxc_902ab47f3194a0a9.text: It became NATO’s 31st member on 4 April 2023.

lxc_870a50c7b7a89850.text: Modern Finland therefore combines local traditions, Nordic democracy, European cooperation, and new security choices.
